briefs.learning_objective: Be able to create and reassign variables to store values using the assignment operator.

required_facts.statement: The equal sign (=) is used to assign a value to a variable.
If a variable has not been assigned a value, trying to use it raises a NameError.
Assigning to a name that already has a value rebinds it to the new value.
A valid variable name is made of letters, digits and the underscore, cannot start with a digit, is case-significant, and is not a reserved keyword such as if, for or class.
An assigned name can be used in a later expression, e.g. after width = 20 and height = 5 * 9, width * height computes using their assigned values.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to recognize and use Python's core scalar data types: int, float, str, and bool.

required_facts.statement: Integer literals (e.g. 2, 4, 20) have type int, and literals with a fractional part (e.g. 5.0, 1.6) have type float.
Text values are of type str (a string) and can be written with single quotes or double quotes with the same result.
The bool type has exactly two values, True and False.
print() writes the value of its arguments; strings are printed without their quotes.
The built-in type() function, called with one argument, returns the type of that object.

optional_enrichment.statement: bool is a subtype of int, so in numeric contexts False and True behave like the integers 0 and 1, though relying on this is discouraged in favor of an explicit int() conversion.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to use Python arithmetic operators for numeric calculations.

required_facts.statement: The operators +, -, * and / perform addition, subtraction, multiplication and division; division (/) always returns a float.
The // operator performs floor division, discarding the fractional part, and the % operator returns the remainder of the division.
The ** operator calculates a power, e.g. 5 ** 2 is 5 squared.
Parentheses can be used to group an expression and control how it is evaluated.
Operators with mixed int/float operands convert the integer operand to floating point, e.g. 4 * 3.75 - 1 evaluates to 14.0.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to compare Python values and produce booleans.

required_facts.statement: The standard comparison operators are <, <=, >, >=, == and !=.
A comparison evaluates to a boolean value: True or False, e.g. 3 < 5 is True.

optional_enrichment.statement: Comparisons can be chained; for example, x < y <= z is equivalent to x < y and y <= z.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to combine boolean conditions with and, or, and not.

required_facts.statement: The Boolean operations, in ascending priority, are or, and, and not.
x or y evaluates to x if x is true, otherwise to y, and is a short-circuit operator that only evaluates y if x is false.
x and y evaluates to x if x is false, otherwise to y, and is a short-circuit operator that only evaluates y if x is true.
not x evaluates to True if x is false, else False; not has a lower priority than the comparison operators, so not a == b is interpreted as not (a == b).

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to convert a value from one core type to another using casting functions like int(), float(), str().

required_facts.statement: The constructors int() and float() can be used to produce a number of a specific type from another value.
int(string) returns an integer object constructed from a string, e.g. int('123') returns 123.
float(string) returns a floating-point number constructed from a string, e.g. float('+1.23') returns 1.23.
Strings may also be created from other objects using the str constructor.

float(string) requires the string to conform to a specific numeric format (an optional sign and digits, optionally with a decimal point or exponent, after surrounding whitespace is removed); not every string can be converted this way.
A string that isn't in the format the target type accepts (for int(), an integer string) raises a ValueError, e.g. int('3.5').

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to branch program execution based on conditions using if/elif/else.

required_facts.statement: An if statement executes its block only when its condition is true.
There can be zero or more elif parts after an if, and the else part is optional; elif is short for 'else if' and helps avoid excessive indentation from nested if statements.
An if/elif/.../else chain selects exactly one suite by evaluating the conditions one by one until one is found to be true; if none of them are true, the else suite (if present) is executed.
Each condition in an if/elif/else chain ends with a colon, and the block belonging to that branch is indented beneath it, e.g. if x < 0: ... elif x == 0: ... else: ....

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to repeat a block of code until a condition becomes false using a while loop.

required_facts.statement: A while loop executes its body repeatedly as long as its condition remains true; the condition can be a comparison, such as a < 10.
The body of a while loop is indented beneath it; in the Fibonacci example, a, b = b, a+b updates a on each pass, and the loop stops once a < 10 becomes false.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to create and manipulate Python's core ordered, mutable data structure: the list.

required_facts.statement: A list is written as a comma-separated sequence of values inside square brackets, e.g. squares = [1, 4, 9, 16, 25].
Like strings, lists can be indexed (squares[0] returns the first item, squares[-1] returns the last) and sliced (squares[-3:] returns a new list of the last three items).
Lists are mutable: an item can be replaced in place, e.g. cubes[3] = 64 changes the value stored at that index.
New items can be added to the end of a list with the list.append() method.

In a slice such as word[0:2], the start index is included and the end index is excluded; lists support the same indexing and slicing operations as strings, e.g. squares[1:3] returns [4, 9], the items from index 1 up to but not including index 3.

optional_enrichment.statement: The built-in function len() returns the number of items in a list.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to create and use Python's core unordered, unique-element data structure: the set.

required_facts.statement: A set is an unordered collection with no duplicate elements, used for membership testing and eliminating duplicate entries.
Curly braces or the set() function create a set; set() must be used for an empty set, because {} creates an empty dictionary instead.
set() can also build a set from the items of another collection, e.g. set('abracadabra') produces the set of unique letters in that string.
The in operator tests membership in a set, e.g. 'orange' in basket.
Set objects support mathematical operations such as union (a | b) and intersection (a & b).

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to create and use Python's core key-value data structure: the dictionary.

required_facts.statement: A dictionary is a collection of key: value pairs, written inside braces, where the keys must be unique within the dictionary.
A value is stored or updated by assigning to a key, e.g. tel['guido'] = 4127, and retrieved by subscripting with the key, e.g. tel['jack'].
Extracting a value for a key that is not in the dictionary by subscripting raises a KeyError.

optional_enrichment.statement: The get() method returns None (or a specified default value) instead of raising an error when a key is not in the dictionary.
The in keyword checks whether a key is present in a dictionary, e.g. 'guido' in tel.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to create string literals and format values into readable strings using f-strings.

required_facts.statement: A quote character can be embedded in a string without escaping it by enclosing the string in the other kind of quote instead, e.g. "doesn't" instead of 'doesn\'t'.
An f-string is a string literal prefixed with f or F that embeds the value of a Python expression inside the string by writing the expression in curly brackets {expression}.

An optional format specifier can follow the expression after a colon, giving greater control over how the value is formatted, such as rounding a number to a chosen number of places after the decimal (e.g. {value:.3f}).

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to define a Python function and call it by name.

required_facts.statement: The keyword def introduces a function definition, followed by the function's name and a parenthesized, possibly empty, list of parameter names, e.g. def my_function():; the statements forming the body start on the next line and must be indented.
A function definition associates the function name with the function object; calling the function by that name (e.g. fib(2000)) runs its body.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to pass values into functions through parameters and arguments.

required_facts.statement: The formal parameters of a function are named in its def statement's parenthesized list.
Inside the function body, each parameter name refers to the argument value that was passed for it when the function was called.
When a function is called with positional arguments, if there are N positional arguments, they are placed in the function's first N parameter slots, in order.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to return a computed value from a function for later reuse.

required_facts.statement: A return statement sends a value back to the code that called the function, e.g. return result gives the caller access to that value.
Even a function without a return statement does return a value: the built-in value None.
The returned value can be stored in a variable for later use, e.g. f100 = fib2(100) stores the list fib2 returns in f100.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to create and use Python's core ordered, immutable data structure: the tuple.

required_facts.statement: A tuple consists of a number of values separated by commas; a tuple's items are shown enclosed in parentheses on output, and a tuple may be written with or without surrounding parentheses as input, e.g. t = 12345, 54321, 'hello!'.
Tuples are immutable: once created, an item inside a tuple cannot be reassigned (t[0] = 88888 raises a TypeError).
A tuple can be unpacked into several variables at once, e.g. x, y, z = t, provided there are as many variables as there are elements in the tuple.

misconceptions.statement: Enclosing a single value in parentheses does not make it a tuple; a one-item tuple requires a trailing comma, e.g. singleton = 'hello',.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to give function parameters default values and call functions using keyword argument syntax.

required_facts.statement: Specifying a default value for a parameter, e.g. def ask_ok(prompt, retries=4):, creates a function that can be called with fewer arguments than it is defined to accept.
A function can also be called using keyword arguments of the form kwarg=value, e.g. parrot(voltage=1000); in a call, keyword arguments must follow any positional arguments.
All the keyword arguments passed in a call must match one of the function's parameters, and no parameter may receive a value more than once.

misconceptions.statement: A default value is evaluated only once, at the point the function is defined, not on each call; if the default is a mutable object such as a list, that same object is shared and can accumulate changes across calls unless the function is written to create a fresh value each time.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to understand how local and global scope determine where a variable name is visible and modifiable.

required_facts.statement: All variable assignments in a function store the value in that function's local symbol table.
For a function that is not nested inside another function, variable references inside it first look in the local symbol table, then the global symbol table, and finally the table of built-in names.
A global variable cannot be directly assigned a value from inside a function unless it is named in a global statement; it may still be referenced (read) without such a statement.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to catch and handle runtime errors gracefully using try/except.

required_facts.statement: The try statement first executes the statements in its try clause; if no exception occurs, the except clause is skipped and execution of the try statement finishes.
If an exception occurs during the try clause and its type matches the exception named after except, the except clause is executed and execution continues after the try/except block.

For example, wrapping int(input(...)) in a try clause with except ValueError lets the program print a message such as 'Oops! That was no valid number. Try again...' instead of crashing when the conversion fails.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to bring code from another module into the current file using import.

required_facts.statement: A module is a file containing Python definitions and statements; definitions from a module can be imported into another module or into the main script with the import statement, e.g. import fibo.
Importing a module this way does not add the names defined in it directly to the current namespace; it adds the module name, so its functions are accessed through that name, e.g. fibo.fib(1000).

The from module import name variant imports names from a module directly into the importing module's namespace, e.g. from fibo import fib, so it can then be called as fib(500) without the module prefix.
Python comes with a library of standard modules that are imported the same way, e.g. import sys makes the sys module's names, such as sys.path, available through sys.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to write idiomatic, PEP 8-compliant Python for readability (naming, spacing, line length).

required_facts.statement: PEP 8 recommends using 4 spaces per indentation level, with spaces rather than tabs as the preferred indentation method.
PEP 8 recommends limiting all lines to a maximum of 79 characters.
PEP 8 recommends avoiding extraneous whitespace, such as immediately inside parentheses/brackets/braces or immediately before a comma, semicolon, or colon.
PEP 8 recommends that function and variable names be lowercase, with words separated by underscores as necessary for readability.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to iterate a known, finite number of times over a sequence using a for loop.

required_facts.statement: Python's for statement iterates over the items of any sequence (such as a list or a string), in the order that they appear in the sequence.
Each pass through a for loop binds the loop variable to the next item of the sequence, e.g. for w in words: print(w, len(w)) prints every word in words.
A for statement's header line ends with a colon, and the statements to repeat are indented beneath it, e.g. for w in words: print(w, len(w)).

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to alter normal loop iteration using break (exit early) and continue (skip to the next iteration).

required_facts.statement: The break statement breaks out of the innermost enclosing for or while loop.
The continue statement continues with the next iteration of the loop, skipping the rest of the current one.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to iterate over the elements of Python's core data structures (lists, dicts, sets, tuples) uniformly.

required_facts.statement: Looping directly over a dictionary (for x in d) yields its keys, since iter(d) returns an iterator over the dictionary's keys.
When looping through a dictionary, the key and its corresponding value can be retrieved together using the items() method, e.g. for k, v in knights.items(): print(k, v).
A set's elements may come out in a different order than expected when iterated over, because a set is unordered.
Tuples are a sequence type, so a for loop visits their items in order the same way it does for a list.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to build a new list or dict in one expression using comprehension syntax.

required_facts.statement: A list comprehension consists of brackets containing an expression followed by a for clause, and optionally more for or if clauses; it produces a new list from evaluating the expression in that context, e.g. [x*2 for x in vec] doubles each value in vec.
A list comprehension can filter its source with an if clause, e.g. [x for x in vec if x >= 0] keeps only the values that satisfy the condition.
Dict comprehensions create dictionaries from arbitrary key and value expressions, e.g. {x: x**2 for x in (2, 4, 6)}.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to read and write text and CSV files from Python using open() and the csv module.

required_facts.statement: open(filename, mode) returns a file object; mode can be 'r' to read, 'w' to write (erasing an existing file of the same name), or 'a' to append, and 'r' is assumed if mode is omitted.
It is good practice to use the with keyword when working with a file object, because it closes the file automatically after its block finishes, even if an exception is raised.
f.read() reads a file's contents and returns them as a string in text mode; once the end of the file is reached, further calls to f.read() return an empty string.
csv.DictReader(f) creates a reader that maps each row of a CSV file to a dict, using the first row's values as keys by default, e.g. for row in reader: print(row['first_name'], row['last_name']).
f.write(string) writes the contents of string to the file, returning the number of characters written.

csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=...) creates a writer that maps a dict to a row; writer.writeheader() writes the header row and writer.writerow(dict) writes one data row, in the order given by fieldnames.
A CSV file used with the csv module should be opened with newline='', e.g. open('names.csv', 'w', newline='').

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to choose a built-in collection for a storage requirement.

required_facts.statement: A list is a mutable sequence whose items can be accessed by position.
A tuple is an immutable sequence whose items can be accessed by position.
A set is a mutable, unordered collection of distinct hashable elements and does not support positional indexing.
A dictionary is mutable, maps unique hashable keys to values and preserves insertion order.
Use d[key] to retrieve a dictionary value by its key, rather than a sequence item by its position.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to implement a simple text-based console interaction.

required_facts.statement: input(prompt) displays the prompt without a trailing newline and returns the entered line as a string with its trailing newline removed.
print(*objects) converts its arguments to strings, separates them with spaces by default and ends with a newline by default.
Store the result of input(prompt) in a name and pass that name alongside greeting text to print to display the entered value.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to iterate over values together with their positions using enumerate.

required_facts.statement: enumerate(sequence, start=0) yields pairs containing a count and the corresponding value; the count starts at zero by default.
Use for position, value in enumerate(sequence, start=1): followed by the loop body to label entries from one without manually updating a counter.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to account for floating-point approximation in numeric comparisons.

required_facts.statement: Many decimal fractions cannot be represented exactly as binary floating-point values, so stored values and arithmetic results can be approximations.
Use math.isclose(actual, expected, rel_tol=..., abs_tol=...) to compare computed floats within chosen relative and absolute tolerances.
math.isclose uses abs(a-b) <= max(rel_tol * max(abs(a), abs(b)), abs_tol), with defaults rel_tol=1e-9 and abs_tol=0.0.
When comparing a nonzero value to zero with math.isclose, supply a positive abs_tol appropriate to the expected closeness.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to use indentation to express Python block structure.

required_facts.statement: Leading whitespace determines the grouping of statements into blocks.
A multiline suite follows its header and colon on indented lines, with statements at the same indentation belonging to the same suite.
Indent a nested header inside the enclosing suite and indent its body further; dedenting ends the nested suite.

optional_enrichment.statement: Mixing tabs and spaces is rejected when the meaning of indentation depends on the worth of a tab in spaces.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to select math functions for a numeric calculation.

required_facts.statement: Import math and call math.sqrt(x) to obtain the square root of x.
math functions operate on real arguments, and the documented implementation raises ValueError for invalid operations such as sqrt(-1.0).

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to access and update values in nested collections.

required_facts.statement: Collections can contain other collections, so each subscription selects one level of the structure.
Use a list index or dictionary key at each successive level, as in records[i][key][j], to reach a nested value.
Assign to the final subscription, as in records[i][key][j] = value, to replace that nested item.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to write and trace nested loops.

required_facts.statement: For each item of an outer for loop, its body runs; an inner for loop reached in that body traverses its items if its execution is uninterrupted, but break exits the innermost enclosing loop early.
Traverse a nested list with for row in rows: and an indented for cell in row: whose further-indented body processes each cell.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to use range for bounded integer iteration.

required_facts.statement: range(stop) starts at zero and uses a step of one, while range(start, stop, step) permits an explicit starting value and stride.
For a positive step, range includes values less than stop; for a negative step, it includes values greater than stop.
Use for i in range(start, stop, 2): to visit every second integer position within a chosen increasing bound.
A range step cannot be zero.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to run a saved Python script with the intended interpreter.

required_facts.statement: Invoke a saved script with the intended Python executable followed by the script path; the interpreter reads and executes that file.
A script runs in a new interpreter invocation, rather than inheriting names from a previous interactive session.
print writes to standard output by default, which is the script output to inspect for displayed results.
An exit status of zero indicates successful termination, while a nonzero status indicates abnormal termination.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to distinguish statements from expressions during Python evaluation.

required_facts.statement: An expression is evaluated to produce a value; an assignment statement binds its target to the resulting object.
Trace an assignment by evaluating the right-hand expression before changing the target binding.
Expressions are evaluated left to right, with operator precedence determining how their parts are grouped.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to write source comments that explain non-obvious intent.

required_facts.statement: A comment starts with # outside a string literal and ends at the end of the physical line; it is ignored by the syntax.
Keep comments consistent with the code and avoid inline comments that merely state the obvious.
Use an inline comment sparingly to explain information that the operation itself does not make obvious.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to use the interactive interpreter to investigate small expressions.

required_facts.statement: Starting the interpreter without a script allows commands to be entered at the interactive prompt.
Interactive expression statements can display computed results, while assignments do not display the assigned values.
Assignments bind names in the session, so later commands can use those names; restart the interpreter to check an expression without earlier bindings.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to explain how Python executes source in a selected runtime.

required_facts.statement: A Python module or interactive command is a code block executed as a unit.
CPython compiles Python source into bytecode instructions that its interpreter executes.
Syntax errors occur while parsing source, whereas exceptions can occur when syntactically correct code executes.
Trace top-level execution in statement order, evaluating the expressions and updating bindings as each executed statement requires.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to continue a Python expression across lines safely.

required_facts.statement: Expressions inside parentheses, square brackets or braces can span physical lines without backslashes.
Reformat a long call by breaking lines inside its argument parentheses while keeping its arguments and operators unchanged.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to transform and split text using string methods.

required_facts.statement: s.strip() returns a copy with leading and trailing whitespace removed, leaving interior whitespace intact.
s.lower() returns a copy with cased characters converted to lowercase.
s.split(sep) returns a list split on the specified delimiter, including empty fields between consecutive delimiters.
s.split() without a separator groups runs of whitespace and omits leading and trailing empty fields.
String methods return transformed values rather than modifying the original string, so assign the returned value when retaining a normalized label.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to distinguish syntax errors from runtime failures.

required_facts.statement: A SyntaxError reports a failure to parse source and can occur before the intended code executes.
An exception can occur while executing a statement or expression that is syntactically correct.
Use the reported source line and location to repair a syntax failure, then rerun to investigate any execution-time exception.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to use Python truth-value rules in conditions.

required_facts.statement: False, None, numeric zero and empty built-in sequences or collections test false; nonempty built-in collections test true.
Use if collection: for a nonempty guard or if not collection: for an empty guard instead of comparing the collection to True.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to check for the absence sentinel None using identity.

required_facts.statement: None is the single object frequently used to represent the absence of a value.
Use value is None or value is not None to check for that object specifically.
A truth-value test also rejects zero and empty values, whereas an identity check against None distinguishes them from absence.
Use mapping.get(key) for an optional lookup; it returns None for a missing key when no other default is supplied, then test the result with is None to preserve a legitimate zero.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to encode and decode between Unicode strings and bytes.

required_facts.statement: str represents Unicode text, whereas bytes represents a sequence of byte values.
text.encode("utf-8") produces UTF-8 bytes, and payload.decode("utf-8") reconstructs text from correctly encoded bytes.
Bytes that are invalid for the chosen encoding can raise UnicodeDecodeError during decoding when errors="strict", the default for bytes.decode().

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to traverse corresponding values from parallel iterables using zip.

required_facts.statement: zip(a, b) yields tuples of corresponding elements and by default stops when the shortest input is exhausted.
Use for left, right in zip(a, b): followed by an indented body to work with paired values.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to avoid unintended collection mutation through aliases and shallow copies.

required_facts.statement: Assignment binds another name to an object rather than copying that object, so mutations through either alias can affect the same collection.
Use list.copy() or a full list slice to create a shallow copy before changing the outer list independently.
A shallow copy creates a new outer collection but retains references to nested objects, so mutating a shared nested object can still affect the original.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to count repeated values with collections.Counter.

required_facts.statement: Import Counter from collections and call Counter(iterable) to count occurrences, with each element as a key and its count as the value.
counter.most_common(1) returns a list containing the most frequent element and its count, or an empty list for an empty counter.
Equal counts in most_common are ordered by first encounter, so a tie does not establish a uniquely most frequent element.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to inspect Python state using temporary diagnostic output.

required_facts.statement: Use labeled print output at relevant execution points to compare observed values with the expected behavior.
repr(value) gives a printable representation that can reveal string quotes and escapes obscured by ordinary display.
Remove temporary diagnostic prints once the problem has been resolved.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to document a reusable Python interface with a docstring.

required_facts.statement: A string literal as the first statement of a function body becomes that function's docstring.
Write a concise summary followed when needed by details of arguments, return values and relevant exceptions, keeping the documentation consistent with the function.
Use help(function) to inspect the function's documentation.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to classify Python exception types by their position in the exception hierarchy.

required_facts.statement: BaseException is the base class of built-in exceptions, while Exception is the base class for non-system-exiting exceptions.
ValueError and OSError are subclasses of Exception, and FileNotFoundError is a subclass of OSError.
KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit inherit directly from BaseException rather than Exception.
Use the documented hierarchy to place an exception beneath its parent instead of treating all exception types as siblings.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to trace exception propagation through function calls.

required_facts.statement: If an exception is not handled in the current function, handling is sought in surrounding execution contexts and callers.
Once an exception interrupts a try suite, its remaining statements are skipped and the first matching except clause is executed.
Trace a call-chain failure from the raising operation outward to the matching handler; an unhandled exception stops execution with an error report.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to guarantee cleanup with finally.

required_facts.statement: A finally suite executes as the try statement is left, whether the try suite succeeds or raises an exception.
Place the resource-release operation in finally after a try suite to perform cleanup when leaving that suite.
A return from try runs finally before returning, while an unhandled exception is re-raised after finally finishes normally.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to pass functions as callback values.

required_facts.statement: A function name refers to a function object that can be assigned to another name or passed as an argument.
Pass transform rather than transform(value) when the receiver needs the callable itself, then call transform(value) inside the receiving helper.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to capture enclosing function state in a closure.

required_facts.statement: A nested function can refer to bindings in an enclosing function scope, retaining access when the nested function is returned.
Use nonlocal name in the nested function to rebind an existing name in the nearest enclosing function scope.
For an independent-state counter factory, initialize the state inside each factory call, define a nested function that updates it using nonlocal, and return that function.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to construct and resolve filesystem paths using pathlib.

required_facts.statement: from pathlib import Path provides path objects with the appropriate concrete path form for the platform.
Join a base path and a relative child with base / child; an absolute child discards preceding path components.
Relative filesystem paths are interpreted from the current working directory, which Path.cwd() reports.
Build a project-relative output path by starting from the chosen project directory rather than assuming the current working directory is that directory.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to raise a meaningful exception for an invalid operation.

required_facts.statement: Use raise ExceptionType(message) to signal a failure explicitly.
ValueError indicates an argument of an appropriate type but an inappropriate value when no more precise exception describes the situation.
Put useful failure context in the exception message so the reported exception explains what was rejected.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to locate Python failures from tracebacks.

required_facts.statement: A traceback shows the execution context leading to an exception, followed by the exception type and explanatory message.
Read the reported file, line and statement for each frame to follow calls toward the failing operation.
Use the final exception description together with the relevant source frame to locate the failure rather than treating the calling line alone as its cause.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to inspect Python execution using breakpoints and stepping.

required_facts.statement: Insert pdb.set_trace() after importing pdb to enter the debugger at the calling frame.
Use p expression to examine a value and where to display the stack.
Use step to enter called functions, next to advance within the current function and continue to resume until a breakpoint.
Use break line to stop at a source line, then inspect the condition values that determine the branch.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to avoid shared mutable function defaults.

required_facts.statement: A default argument value is evaluated once at function definition, so a mutable default object can be shared across calls.
Replace a default list with a None default and create a new list inside the function when the argument is None.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to order iterable values using a key function.

required_facts.statement: sorted(iterable, key=function) returns a new sorted list, whereas list.sort(key=function) changes the list in place.
The key callable receives each item and provides the value used for sorting, so pass a function that derives the required normalized key.
Sorting is stable: items with equal keys retain their original relative order.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to write a small anonymous callable using lambda.

required_facts.statement: lambda parameters: expression creates a function whose result is that expression, without a statement body.
Pass key=lambda item: expression to a sorting operation to supply a one-expression key transformation.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to select and order specific Python exception handlers.

required_facts.statement: An except clause matches its named exception class and subclasses, and the first matching clause handles the exception.
Place except FileNotFoundError: before except OSError: to keep the specific recovery branch reachable for missing files.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to diagnose whether a Python failure comes from invalid input, an implementation defect or an external operational problem.

required_facts.statement: int(text) raises ValueError for text that does not represent a valid integer; catch it at the input boundary and report rejection when the contract requires a numeric input.
NameError means a local or global name was not found; a misspelled local name should be corrected in the implementation rather than attributed to malformed numeric input.
PermissionError indicates inadequate access rights, so a valid path can still require an external-permission failure response rather than input rejection or assuming a coding defect.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to bind variable arguments using *args and **kwargs.

required_facts.statement: A parameter of the form *args collects additional positional arguments into a tuple, while **kwargs collects additional keyword arguments into a dictionary.
Forward collected arguments with target(*args, **kwargs), using * to expand positional values and ** to expand named values.
Passing more than one value for the same parameter, including a positional value and a keyword value, raises TypeError.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to define classes and create ordinary instances.

required_facts.statement: Use class Name: followed by an indented body to define a class object.
Calling a class, as in Name(), creates an instance of that class.
Two ordinary class-instantiation calls produce distinct instance objects; is compares their identities rather than merely their class.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to select Python file modes without unintended data loss.

required_facts.statement: open(path, "r") opens for reading and is the default mode.
open(path, "w") truncates an existing file, while open(path, "a") appends to the end.
open(path, "x") creates a file exclusively and fails if the destination already exists.
Catch FileExistsError around exclusive creation to handle an existing report destination without truncating it.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to initialize per-instance state with __init__.

required_facts.statement: When a class defines __init__, class instantiation calls it on the new instance with the supplied arguments.
Define def __init__(self, name, quantity): and assign self.name = name and self.quantity = quantity in its body to store each instance's initial values.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to implement instance behavior using self.

required_facts.statement: A method called as instance.method(arguments) receives the instance as its first argument, conventionally named self.
Define def method(self, ...): in the class and use self.attribute to read or assign the receiving object's stored state.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to choose the method binding appropriate to an object's operation.

required_facts.statement: An instance method receives the instance, a @classmethod receives the class as its first argument, and a @staticmethod receives no implicit first argument.
Use @classmethod above def constructor(cls, ...): and return cls(...) to provide an alternative constructor tied to the receiving class.
Use @staticmethod above a function that requires neither instance nor class state.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to combine collaborating objects through composition.

required_facts.statement: An instance attribute can refer to another object, making that object a contained collaborator rather than an inherited base.
Store a collaborator with self.collaborator = collaborator and delegate with self.collaborator.method(...) when its behavior is needed.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to apply Python conventions for non-public object state.

required_facts.statement: Prefix an implementation attribute with a single underscore to mark it as a non-public API detail that may change.
Expose intended operations as public methods while accessing supporting state through the implementation; underscore naming is a convention, not enforced access security.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to extend inherited behavior using super().

required_facts.statement: class Derived(Base): defines a subclass that can inherit base-class attributes and override methods by defining them again.
Use super().method(...) in an overriding method to delegate according to the method resolution order rather than hard-coding a parent.
When defining a subclass __init__, call super().__init__(...) to retain the base initialization behavior before adding the subclass's state.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to define an application-specific exception type.

required_facts.statement: Define class InvalidRecordError(Exception): with an indented body to create an exception type for a domain failure.
Raise InvalidRecordError(message) at the validation failure and catch except InvalidRecordError: where the caller can respond to it.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to distinguish instance state from shared class attributes.

required_facts.statement: Class variables hold shared attributes, while attributes assigned on self can store data unique to an instance.
A mutable list defined in the class body can be shared by instances, so append operations can unexpectedly affect other instances.
Initialize self.items = [] inside __init__ to give each instance its own list instead of mutating a shared class list.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to serialize and deserialize supported Python data using the json module.

required_facts.statement: json.dumps(record) serializes supported Python values to a JSON string and json.loads(text) reconstructs Python values from a JSON string.
JSON objects decode to dict, arrays to list, strings to str, booleans to bool and null to None.
Python lists and tuples both encode as JSON arrays, so a tuple decodes back as a list.
JSON object keys are strings, so a dictionary with non-string keys need not equal the dictionary obtained after serialization and reconstruction.
Compare the reconstructed nested values and types with the conversion table rather than assuming round-tripping preserves every Python-specific type.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to inspect Python object types and attributes.

required_facts.statement: type(obj) returns an object's type.
isinstance(obj, Class) tests whether the object is an instance of the class or one of its subclasses.
dir(obj) produces a list of attribute names useful for inspection, but its output is not necessarily complete.
Inspect public candidate attributes by selecting names from dir(obj) that do not start with an underscore.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to perform filesystem operations using pathlib.

required_facts.statement: Path.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) creates a directory and needed parents, allowing an existing directory but not an existing non-directory at that path.
Path.iterdir() yields the directory's child paths in arbitrary order.
source.rename(target) renames a filesystem entry to the specified target and returns a new path pointing there.
A relative rename target is interpreted from the current working directory, and an existing target file is replaced on Unix but raises FileExistsError on Windows.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to define readable object representations using special methods.

required_facts.statement: __repr__(self) returns a string intended as an information-rich and unambiguous representation, useful for debugging.
__str__(self) returns a string intended as a convenient printable representation for str and print.
Define both methods to return strings when the developer representation and user-facing display should differ.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to specify the encoding contract for text-file access.

required_facts.statement: Open a text file with encoding="utf-8" when its contents are UTF-8, since the unspecified default encoding is platform-dependent.
Use text-mode read and write operations with the matching explicit encoding on both files to preserve non-ASCII text.
A UnicodeDecodeError indicates a decoding failure; check whether the chosen encoding matches the file's actual bytes.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to handle expected file and parsing failures at a Python I/O boundary.

required_facts.statement: FileNotFoundError indicates a requested file or directory does not exist; handle it separately from failures in the file's contents.
UnicodeDecodeError identifies bytes that could not be decoded, so report the decoding problem rather than labeling the file missing.
csv.reader(file, strict=True) raises csv.Error on bad CSV input; use except csv.Error: and reader.line_num when reporting the failure location.
A CSV parser returns fields as strings by default; check len(row) and required field values against the input contract and handle ValueError from invalid numeric conversion separately.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to manage resource lifetimes using with.

required_facts.statement: A with statement enters a context manager before the suite and invokes its exit operation when the suite finishes or raises.
Use with open(path, mode) as file: followed by an indented processing suite to close the file automatically on exit.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to read and write bytes through binary file streams.

required_facts.statement: Open files with "rb" for binary reading and "wb" for binary writing; these operations handle bytes rather than text strings.
Read the payload from the binary source and pass those bytes directly to the binary destination's write method without decoding or encoding.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to calculate date and time differences with datetime.

required_facts.statement: datetime.strptime(text, format) parses a date-time string according to a supplied format; %Y-%m-%d specifies a four-digit year, month and day.
Subtract compatible datetime values to obtain a timedelta representing their difference.
Use delta.days to obtain the day component of a timedelta; for parsed midnight calendar dates it represents their whole-day difference.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to extract reusable code into a local Python module.

required_facts.statement: A module is a file containing Python definitions and statements, with its module name normally derived from its .py filename.
Put a helper definition in helper_module.py and use import helper_module followed by helper_module.helper(...) from a sibling script.
A module has its own namespace; its executable top-level statements run on its first import in a session.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to organize local importable Python packages.

required_facts.statement: A regular package uses a directory containing __init__.py and its related module files.
Import a helper module with import package.module and call package.module.helper(...) to use its qualified name.
The __init__.py file can be empty or execute package initialization code.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to report program events using logging.

required_facts.statement: Use logger = logging.getLogger(__name__) after importing logging to obtain a module-named logger.

Emit events with logger.debug for detailed diagnostic information, logger.info to confirm expected operation, logger.warning for unexpected events or possible problems while software still works, logger.error when a serious problem prevents a function, or logger.critical when a serious error may prevent the program from continuing; events below the effective logging level are not processed.
Configure logging once for the application, for example with logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO), rather than adding a handler on each helper call.
Attaching handlers to both a logger and its ancestors can emit the same event multiple times because propagation is enabled by default.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to separate importable definitions from script-only execution.

required_facts.statement: A module executed as the top-level program has __name__ equal to "__main__", while an imported module has its module name.
Place command-interface invocation under if __name__ == "__main__": so imports define the helper without running that invocation.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to parse a script's command-line interface with argparse.

required_facts.statement: Create argparse.ArgumentParser(), register arguments with add_argument and call parse_args() to obtain an object holding parsed values.
add_argument("input_path") declares a positional argument that is required by default, while add_argument("--verbose", action="store_true") declares an optional boolean flag.
Use args.input_path and args.verbose from the parsed object to drive the script's processing and verbosity.
parse_args reports invalid invocations such as missing required arguments and exits with status 2 by default.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to diagnose Python module discovery and name shadowing.

required_facts.statement: Python resolves imports using its module search path; the script directory or current directory can precede installed standard-library modules.
Inspect sys.path to see search locations and module.__file__ to see the file used for a file-backed imported module.
Rename a local file that shadows a standard-library module and retry in a fresh interpreter so an earlier cached import does not conceal the correction.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to read environment-variable configuration with os.environ.

required_facts.statement: os.environ is a mapping of the process's environment variables to string values.
Use os.environ.get("SETTING", fallback) to retrieve a nonsecret configuration value with a fallback when absent.
For a required setting, retrieve it without a fallback and explicitly reject None rather than silently continuing with a missing value.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to choose random or secrets according to the use of randomness.

required_facts.statement: random generates pseudo-random values for modeling and simulation, not security-sensitive purposes.
Initialize random.Random(seed) and use its methods for a repeatable simulation sequence with the same seed and compatible generator behavior, without concurrent threads changing its state.
Use secrets.token_hex(nbytes) or secrets.token_urlsafe(nbytes) for security-sensitive tokens rather than random.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to recognize simple text patterns using re.

required_facts.statement: Square brackets specify a character class, ranges such as [a-z] specify allowed characters, and * permits zero or more repetitions while + requires one or more.
Use re.fullmatch(pattern, text) to require the entire text to match; it returns a match object on success and None otherwise.

Construct an identifier-like pattern from a character class for allowed initial characters followed by a character class for allowed remaining characters repeated with *; use a raw string for the pattern.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to inspect interpreter runtime information using sys.

required_facts.statement: sys.executable normally gives the absolute path of the running interpreter executable, but can be empty or None if Python cannot retrieve it.
sys.version is a string containing the Python version and additional build information.
Import sys and print labeled sys.executable and sys.version values to identify the actual running runtime.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to create and use an isolated Python virtual environment.

required_facts.statement: A virtual environment provides its own interpreter entry points and, by default, packages isolated from other environments.
Create an environment with python -m venv .venv using the selected base interpreter.
Use .venv/bin/python on POSIX or .venv\Scripts\python.exe on Windows, or activate the environment to put its executables on PATH.
Verify the running executable with sys.executable and inspect installed packages with the environment interpreter's -m pip list command.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to select and verify the interpreter used for a Python project.

required_facts.statement: An environment's Python executable can be invoked directly without activation; activation changes PATH to select it for shell commands.
Inspect sys.executable in the running program to verify which interpreter a terminal or editor actually selected.
When an editor runs the wrong interpreter, select the intended environment's executable in its run configuration and rerun the diagnostic.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to install dependencies using the intended Python environment's pip.

required_facts.statement: Use the intended interpreter with python -m pip install PackageName to install into that interpreter's environment.
Use python -m pip show PackageName or python -m pip list with the same interpreter to inspect the installed package.
Verify the documented import with that environment's interpreter; an installed distribution name and its import name need not be identical.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to recreate an environment's dependencies from a requirements file.

required_facts.statement: A requirements file lists packages to install; PackageName==version pins a specific version.
Use the target environment's python -m pip install -r requirements.txt to install the listed requirements.
Use the same environment's python -m pip list and documented imports to check that the recreated environment has the intended dependencies.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to use assert to express development-only invariants.

required_facts.statement: assert condition raises AssertionError if the condition is false; assert condition, message supplies an explanatory value.
Use assert for an internal invariant that should hold during development, not for required public-input validation.
Assertions may be omitted when Python is run with optimization, so enforce required input checks with explicit conditionals and exceptions.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to distinguish iterables from iterators.

required_facts.statement: An iterable can supply an iterator through iter(iterable); an iterator maintains traversal state and next(iterator) returns its next item.
next(iterator) raises StopIteration after the items are exhausted unless a default is supplied.
Two calls to iter(a_list) create independent traversal states, while iter(an_iterator) returns the iterator itself.
Store two list iterators in separate names and call next on each to advance their positions independently.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to produce lazy values with yield.

required_facts.statement: A function containing yield produces a generator iterator when called rather than running its body to completion immediately.
yield value suspends the function and retains local state, resuming after that yield when the next item is requested.
To yield valid records lazily, loop over the input and yield each record inside the required validity condition.
Returning or reaching the end of the generator function ends iteration.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to write generator expressions for lazy transformations.

required_facts.statement: A generator expression uses (expression for item in iterable if condition) to transform and optionally filter items lazily.
Pass a generator expression to sum, as in sum(transform(item) for item in records if condition(item)), to accumulate values without creating an intermediate list.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to account for iterator consumption and exhaustion.

required_facts.statement: Each next call consumes one iterator item, so later traversal continues from its current position rather than restarting.
An exhausted iterator must continue to raise StopIteration on later requests.
To repeat traversal, obtain a new iterator from a reusable iterable or retain items in a collection before consuming the iterator.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to choose eager or lazy processing for an iterable workload.

required_facts.statement: A list comprehension constructs a list eagerly, whereas a generator expression supplies values during iteration.
Prefer a generator expression for a one-pass aggregation when retaining an intermediate list is unnecessary.
Materialize with list(iterable) when retained values are needed for repeated traversal, accepting the memory cost of storing them.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to chain iterable inputs lazily using itertools.chain.

required_facts.statement: itertools.chain(*iterables) yields all elements from the first input, then the next inputs in sequence, without constructing a concatenated list.
Import chain from itertools and traverse chain(first, second), or pass it to the aggregation, to combine sources in one lazy traversal.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to choose a readable iterable transformation idiom.

required_facts.statement: map(function, iterable) returns an iterator applying the function to each item.
filter(function, iterable) returns an iterator of items whose predicate result tests true; filter(None, iterable) keeps truthy items.
Use [transform(item) for item in iterable if predicate(item)] for a readable eager transformation and filtering operation, or parentheses for a lazy generator expression.
Passing an existing callable to map or filter avoids a wrapper expression; a comprehension can state the equivalent transformation and condition together.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to express supplied checks in Python unittest.TestCase syntax.

required_facts.statement: Define a subclass of unittest.TestCase with methods whose names begin with test to express individual checks.
Use self.assertEqual(actual, expected) for equality checks and self.assertTrue(condition) for truth checks.
Use with self.assertRaises(ExceptionType): around the tested call to check that supplied invalid input raises the expected exception.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to run Python unittest discovery and interpret runner outcomes.

required_facts.statement: Run python -m unittest test_module for a named module or python -m unittest discover to find tests.
Discovery looks for test*.py by default and loads matching test cases; inspect the reported test count so zero discovered tests is not mistaken for executed checks.
A failure is a failed assertion, whereas an error is an unexpected exception from a test.
Read the FAIL or ERROR entry, traceback and final counts to locate a failing test and distinguish it from successful checks.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to implement isolated unittest fixtures with setup and cleanup hooks.

required_facts.statement: setUp runs before each test method, so create fresh mutable fixture state there instead of sharing state between tests.
Register resource release with self.addCleanup(function, *args, **kwargs); cleanup functions run in reverse registration order.
tearDown runs after a test when setUp succeeded, while registered cleanups still run if setUp fails.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to explain generated code in terms of the stated requirements.

required_facts.statement: Read the implementation line by line and check that it matches the intended behavior rather than assuming its apparent plausibility establishes correctness.
Trace the values and branches for a supplied valid and invalid input, comparing the observed return or exception with the stated requirement.
Test code obtained from a virtual assistant instead of relying on the response alone.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to check generated Python code for destructive filesystem behavior.

required_facts.statement: Opening an existing file with "w" truncates it, so inspect write modes before executing code that must preserve existing contents.
Path.unlink removes a file or symbolic link and Path.rmdir removes an empty directory, so inspect deletion calls and their targets before running a cleanup helper.
Relative paths depend on the current working directory; inspect the resolved target to identify unintended filesystem locations.
Remove an unintended deletion call rather than executing it to discover its effect.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to reject unsafe execution of untrusted input in generated Python code.

required_facts.statement: eval evaluates Python expressions and exec executes Python code; passing user-supplied input to either can execute arbitrary code.
For numeric input, use explicit conversion such as int(text) and handle ValueError rather than evaluating the text as Python code.
When explicitly invoking a shell, shell metacharacters and whitespace in untrusted input must be accounted for to avoid shell injection; prefer an argument sequence without shell=True.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to check generated Python API claims in authoritative documentation.

required_facts.statement: Check the claimed API in its official reference entry, including the documented parameter signature and return-value description.
Compare the generated call with that entry's positional and keyword argument rules, defaults and supported inputs rather than inferring them from its name.
Use help(object) to inspect available documentation, then test the documented behavior with the interpreter version used by the project.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to verify suggested dependencies before installation.

required_facts.statement: Distinguish a distribution package installed by pip from the import package used in Python; the names can differ.
Before installation, compare the suggested distribution name and version with the project's documented dependency requirement and package source rather than treating a plausible name as sufficient.
pip can install from PyPI, other indexes or specified sources, so check which source the proposed installation command actually uses.

Do not install a distribution merely because its name matches a generated import: indexes do not enforce that relationship, and a blind installation can select an unintended or malicious package. Confirm its documented identity and intended use first.

briefs.learning_objective: Be able to decide whether generated Python code is acceptable using evidence.

required_facts.statement: Treat generated code as an implementation to read and test against the intended behavior, not as established correctness.
For acceptance, cite the supplied checks of required behavior and the resolved safety findings rather than relying on how plausible the implementation looks.
Choose repair for an identified correctable defect, then rerun the relevant checks before reconsidering acceptance.
For rejection, identify the unresolved failed requirement or unsafe operation and record that finding as the reason, rather than claiming the implementation is correct.
